narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is the closing charge of the psalm: 'Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait' (chazaq) - strength summoned as a command, not described as a possession. Type (102) is volition: this is not a felt state nor a bare deed but an act of the will, strength commanded into being, the interior told to brace itself. Source (103) is absent: the reading does not trace where the strength is to come from - it does not book God, the LORD's steadfast love, or past rescue as its origin, though the whole psalm has just rehearsed them; the row reports the summons, not its supply, leaving the strength's spring unaccounted and resting the whole weight on the act of willing. Seat (104) resolves to none: for all that 'heart' is named in the verse, the operation is not treated as organ-located - 'heart' reads as the whole inner person rallying itself, not a faculty-organ being switched on, so the strength is held by the person as such rather than lodged in an interior seat. Bearer (105) is 'those who wait' (inferred, to_span 276809): the interior addressed is the waiting one - not the strong-already but those still holding out for the LORD, the community of hope the psalmist turns to at the end. Operation (106), the core event, is 'the self exhorts all who wait for the LORD to be strong and let their heart take courage' - a self-and-communal command to steadfast hope; the movement is the psalmist's interior turning outward to brace every other waiting interior. Target (107) is exhortation (inferred, to_span 276809): what the operation aims at is the rousing itself - the object is the act of urging courage into the waiting, a reflexive charge that the hopeful summon strength. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - not strained, not easy, not fierce; the command stands flatly, and that flatness presents the summoning of strength as plain duty rather than a feat wrung out under pressure. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree of the strength is measured, nothing narrows or particularises it beyond 'be strong', and no downstream outcome is booked - the reading leaves the strength as a commanded posture, not scored and not followed to a result. Coupling (112) is 'strong-in-waiting' (inferred, to_span 276809): the one binding the reading registers is the weld of strength to waiting - the two are inseparable, for this is not the strength of action but the strength that holds while it waits; courage is the form endurance takes. Prohibition (113) is absent: this is a positive charge, not a forbidding. Discovery (114) names the placement: the operation closes the psalm by commanding the waiting interior to summon strength - hope braced with courage. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait the inner being is charged to hold, not a passing surge. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the whole thing sits inside, a condition of the inner life the will is told to enter. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist's interior turns outward and commands every waiting interior to will itself strong and let the heart take courage - a strength that is volitional, welded to waiting, reported without degree or strain, and lodged wholly within as the posture of those who hope for the LORD.
narratives.story: The psalm has run its long course of danger, distress, and rescue, and it ends not with a description but with a command: be strong, and let your heart take courage, all of you who are still waiting for the Lord. Strength here is something willed, not something you simply have - the inner self is told to brace itself. And it is aimed outward, to everyone else who waits: the psalmist rallies the whole company of the hopeful. Notice what the strength is bound to - waiting. This is not the strength of charging into battle but the strength of holding on, the courage that keeps a heart steady while it waits. The passage never says where the strength is supposed to come from, though the whole psalm has just been full of God's rescuing love; it simply issues the charge and leaves the summoning to the will. There is no strain in it and no reward tacked on - just a plain call to every waiting person to take heart and hold firm.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chayil - 'With God we shall do valiantly': valour, doing with strength, the vigour that carries a people into action. Type (102) is action: this is a doing, not a felt state - valiant conduct, deeds done with force. Source (103) carries a real value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 280798 to_span 280800): 'because it is God who treads down our foes' - the valour's spring is named and it is not the people themselves; the strength that lets them act is sourced in God's own treading-down of the enemy. Seat (104) is none: the valour is not organ-located, not lodged in an interior faculty - it is the people's action, not the working of an inner organ. Bearer (105) is the people (inferred, to_span 280798): the collective interior of the nation, the 'we' who will do valiantly, read against the psalm's despair that God has rejected them and does not march with their armies. Operation (106) is 'do valiantly / act with valor': the event is the valiant doing itself. Target (107) is none: the reading books no object the valour is aimed at - it is not directed at a named foe or good but reported as the mode of the people's own acting, its force turned into deed rather than pointed at a target. Manner (108) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 280798 to_span 280800): 'with God, who treads down the foes' - the HOW is marked, and it marks the valour as done in company with God, whose act underwrites theirs; the valour never operates alone but always 'with God'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree of the valour is scored, nothing further particularises it, and no separate outcome is booked - the treading-down of foes belongs to God as source and manner, not filed as this operation's downstream effect. Coupling (112) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 280798 to_span 280793): it is 'the positive counterpart to man's vain salvation' (v11) - the valour is welded in direct contrast to the vanity of human help; where man's salvation is empty, the God-founded valour is the answering reality, the two set as opposites. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) is decisive: this is 'the God-founded courage that closes the lament' - chayil here the valour that is not self-confidence but confidence in God, the very word used for the enemy's 'power' now made the people's, because God himself treads down the foe (the qualifier). Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the delivered people, not a one-off surge. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the valour is a condition of the inner life, held within the people even as it issues in outward deed. The full process: a people who feel abandoned by God turn, at the psalm's close, to a valour sourced in God's own treading-down of their foes and exercised only 'with God' - a doing without a booked target, welded as the exact positive counterpart to the vanity of human rescue, held as an inner state that is confidence in God, not in themselves.
narratives.story: The prayer has been bleak: God seems to have rejected his people and no longer goes out with their armies, and human help, they say, is worthless. Then the tone turns at the very end - with God, they declare, we shall do valiantly. The courage they claim is real strength for real action, but its source is named plainly, and it is not themselves: they can act boldly only because God is the one who tramples their enemies. The valour is always exercised in his company, never on its own. And it is set as the exact opposite of the empty human rescue they had just dismissed - where man's help is vain, this God-backed boldness is the answer that actually holds. Strikingly, it is the same kind of strength the enemy was said to wield, now turned into the people's, but only because God fights for them. So the courage is genuine and it moves them to act, yet at heart it is confidence in God rather than in their own arm.
narratives.variation_note: The same refrain, 'With God we shall do valiantly', recurs at Psa 108:13 (reading H2428:valiantly#2) in a near-identical psalm, yet the two readings differ in coding and emphasis, and the difference is itself the finding. Here at Psa 60:12 the valour is read as an ACTION whose source and manner are both explicitly booked to God ('because it is God who treads down our foes'; 'with God, who treads down the foes'), and it is coupled directly as the positive counterpart to man's vain salvation, located as an internal ib-state. At Psa 108:13 the same words are read as a DISPOSITION: source and manner are left unbooked (none), the target is oriented 'through God', and the locus is set against 'the vanity of human help'. Both ground valour in God rather than self - the substance is one - but this reading foregrounds the deed and God's answering act, while the other foregrounds the settled bearing and its orientation, showing how one refrain can be weighted now as a God-empowered doing, now as a God-oriented disposition.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chazaq - 'They hold fast to their evil purpose': to grip, to strengthen oneself, to brace and cling. Read without valence-filtering, this is steadfastness in its dark form - the same holding-firm that elsewhere braces hope here bracing wickedness. Type (102) is action: a doing, the active clinging and mutual bracing of the wicked, not a mere feeling. Source (103) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 281127 to_span 306458): 'until God shoots his arrow at them (v7)' - the reading traces the term of this holding-fast not to an interior spring but to its outer limit, the point where God's counter-arrow will break it; the clinging runs on until God ends it. Seat (104) is none: the holding-fast is not organ-located, not lodged in a named inner faculty - it is the persons' resolve, not the malfunction of an interior organ. Bearer (105) is the wicked (inferred, to_span 281127): this is the interior of the evildoers, the throng who whet their tongues and shoot from ambush, read from within. Operation (106) is 'hold fast / strengthen themselves in': the event is the resolute gripping, the wicked bracing one another in their aim. Target (107) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 281127 to_span 281128): 'their evil purpose' - what they hold fast to is the wicked scheme itself; the clinging is aimed squarely at their evil design. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - the flat report withholds any 'how', presenting the entrenchment as bare fact rather than colouring it. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree of the resolve is scored, nothing narrows it, and no downstream outcome is booked to the operation - the shattering of v7 is read as source/limit, not filed as this act's effect. Coupling (112) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 281127 to_span 281128): it is 'paired with the evil purpose they cling to' - the holding-fast is welded to the very scheme it grips; resolve and object are inseparable, the strength existing only as strength-toward-evil. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: this is 'the resolute, mutually-encouraged clinging to wickedness' - chazaq here the enemies bracing one another in evil, entrenched in their scheme, a determined wickedness that God's counter-arrow will shatter (v7). Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the wicked's interior, not a passing impulse. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the resolve is a condition of the inner life, an entrenched inward bracing even as it issues in ambush. The full process: from no named interior source and no organ-seat, the wicked grip and strengthen one another in their evil purpose, welding their resolve to that very scheme, a determined inward steadfastness aimed at wickedness that runs on until God's arrow breaks it. This is the family's steadfastness read in descent - the same holding-firm, turned to evil, and shown to have a hard outer limit in God.
narratives.story: This psalm looks straight into the inner world of wrongdoers. They whet their tongues like swords and shoot their words from ambush, and at the centre of the picture is their resolve: they hold fast to their evil plan. It is the very same grip that, in a good person, would be steadfast courage - but here it is bent toward wickedness. They brace and encourage one another, digging in, determined, and their determination is inseparable from the scheme itself: the strength exists only as strength for doing harm. The passage does not soften this or explain it away; it simply reports the entrenched resolve as fact. Yet it also marks where such stubborn evil runs out - it holds on only until God shoots his own arrow at them and shatters it. Their firmness is real, but it has a hard limit, and the limit is God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is oz - 'Blessed are those whose strength is in you': strength named not as a capacity a person owns but as one located in God. Type (102) is disposition: not a single act nor a felt spike but a settled bearing, a standing leaning of the inner being. Source (103) is absent: the reading does not book a separate origin behind the disposition - though the verse itself says the strength is 'in you', the source-row is left empty, so the strength's supply is reported through its locus rather than traced as an intake event. Seat (104) is none: the strength is not organ-located, not lodged in an interior faculty - it is the person's leaning, held by the whole self rather than seated in an inner organ. Bearer (105) is the pilgrim (inferred, to_span 284107): the interior of the traveller to Zion, the one 'in whose heart are the highways', read as he sets out. Operation (106) is 'find strength': the event is the discovery and drawing of strength - not generating it from within but locating it in God. Target (107) is 'in God' (inferred, to_span 284107): the object the strength rests in is God himself; the interior reaches out and grounds its power there, not in its own resources. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - the leaning is stated plainly, without qualifier of struggle or ease. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree of the strength is scored, nothing further particularises it, and no downstream outcome is booked - the reading holds it as a settled disposition, not a measured or consequence-bearing act. Coupling (112) carries a value (inferred, to_span 284107): it is 'paired with the heart set on Zion' - the strength-in-God is welded to the pilgrim's inward orientation, the highways to Zion in the heart; the power and the longing move together, the strength being the strength of a heart already bent toward the sanctuary. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'those whose strength is in you' - reliance on God as one's power, the inner leaning that sustains the journey. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the pilgrim's inner being. Locus (116) is external:god - and this is the sharpest finding: unlike most readings in the family, the strength does not sit inside the person as an ib-state but is located OUTSIDE, in God; its reference-point is external, the power borrowed from another. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the pilgrim finds his strength not in himself but in God, resting his power there and welding it to a heart already set on Zion - a settled disposition of reliance whose very locus is external, the strength of one who leans on God to carry him the whole way.
narratives.story: This is a psalm of pilgrims longing for God's house, and one line quietly names what keeps them going: their strength is in God. It is not power they carry in themselves and spend along the road; it is strength they find by leaning on him. The person pictured is a traveller whose heart is already set on the journey to Zion, and his strength and his longing move together - it is the strength of a heart bent toward the place it loves. What is most striking is where that strength actually lives: not inside him as his own reserve, but outside him, in God, borrowed and drawn on step by step. The passage does not describe him working it up or straining for it; it simply calls him blessed, a man whose power for the long road is God himself.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chayil - 'They go from strength to strength': strength as mounting vigour, power that increases rather than drains as the journey goes on. Type (102) is state: a condition the pilgrims are in, not a single deed - the growing strength itself. Source (103) is absent: the reading does not book a separate origin for the mounting vigour - the renewal is reported as a state, not traced to a named supply, though the whole psalm places it in the God the pilgrims approach. Seat (104) is none: the strength is not organ-located, not lodged in an interior faculty - it is the pilgrims' condition, held by the persons rather than seated in an inner organ. Bearer (105) is the pilgrims (inferred, to_span 284122): the interior of the travellers as a body, the ones crossing the Valley of Baca toward Zion. Operation (106) is 'go from strength to strength': the event is the increase itself, strength renewed and compounding stride by stride. Target (107) is 'toward God' (inferred, to_span 284122): the strength is oriented forward, its increase pointed at the goal of appearing before God in Zion; the vigour moves Godward. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - the mounting is stated plainly, without qualifier. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree beyond 'from strength to strength' is scored, nothing further particularises it, and no separate outcome is booked - the increase is held as a state, not followed to a filed result. Coupling (112) carries a value (inferred, to_span 284122): it is 'paired with appearing before God' - the mounting strength is welded to the journey's end, each one appearing before God in Zion; the growth and the arrival belong together, strength increasing precisely as the presence nears. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'they go from strength to strength' - the mounting vigour of the pilgrim, renewed not drained as Zion nears. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the pilgrim body on the way. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - unlike the oz of v5, whose locus was external in God, this chayil sits inside the pilgrims as their own renewing condition, an inner state of increase. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the pilgrims move through a hard valley and, instead of tiring, grow - strength compounding stride by stride, oriented toward God and welded to the coming appearance before him in Zion, an inner state of mounting vigour that swells as the goal draws near.
narratives.story: In the same pilgrim psalm, a few lines on, the travellers are crossing a dry, hard valley on their way to God's house - and instead of wearing out, they grow stronger. They go, the psalm says, from strength to strength: the closer they come, the more vigour they have, renewed rather than drained by the road. It is a condition they are in, a rising energy that builds with every mile. And it is bound up with where they are headed - each of them will at last appear before God in Zion, and the strength swells precisely because that meeting is drawing near. Here the strength is felt as something inside them, their own renewing life, even though it is the destination that keeps refilling it. The picture is of pilgrims who should be exhausted but are instead gathering power as they approach the God they long to see.
narratives.variation_note: Psa 84 holds two distinct strength-readings and the study must not collapse them - the difference between them is a finding. At v5 the term is oz (H5797:strength#1), read as a settled DISPOSITION of reliance whose locus is EXTERNAL, in God: strength found by leaning outward. Here at v7 the term is chayil (H2428:strength#1), read as a STATE of mounting vigour whose locus is INTERNAL to the pilgrims: strength felt as their own renewing condition. The one is where the strength is grounded (in God); the other is how it is experienced on the road (rising within). Together they show a single pilgrimage carried by a strength that is God's in its source yet increasingly the traveller's own as the presence nears.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is eyal - 'I am a man who has no strength': strength named only by its absence, vitality reported as gone. Read without valence-bias, this is the family's word for power read at its nadir - strength present in the text purely as a lack. Type (102) is state: a condition the sufferer is in, the settled state of depletion, not an act. Source (103) is absent: the reading does not book an origin for the loss - it does not name what drained the strength; the powerlessness is reported as a bare state, its cause unfiled, which fits a sufferer who can no longer even account for his ruin. Seat (104) is none: the strengthlessness is not organ-located, not lodged in a named inner faculty - it is the whole man emptied, not one organ failing. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred, to_span 284485): the first-person interior of the sufferer, the one crying day and night, counted among those going down to the pit. Operation (106) is 'have no strength': the event is a negation - the non-possession of vitality, an absence where strength should be. Target (107) is 'against death' (inferred, to_span 284485): the strength that is missing is missing precisely as power to resist death - there is nothing in him to push back against the grave he is sinking toward. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - the emptiness is stated flatly, without qualifier, the bare fact of a man with nothing left. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree of the depletion is scored beyond 'no strength', nothing narrows it, and no separate outcome is booked - the powerlessness simply IS his state, not followed to a filed consequence. Coupling (112) carries a value (inferred, to_span 284485): it is 'paired with being counted dead' - the strengthlessness is welded to his reckoning among the dead, like the slain in the grave; the lack of vitality and the status of already-as-good-as-dead are one condition. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'I am a man who has no strength' - the utter powerlessness of the sufferer, vitality gone. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of his present state, the settled condition of the psalm, not a passing dip. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the emptiness is a condition of the inner life, felt within as the draining-away of the man's own vitality. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the sufferer registers strength only as its absence - a man with nothing left to resist death, his powerlessness welded to his being counted among the dead, an inner state of total depletion. This is the descent-pole of the family: not strength summoned or increasing but strength wholly gone, the interior emptied at the edge of the grave.
narratives.story: This is one of the darkest psalms, and its speaker is a man at the end of himself. He cries out to God day and night, but he describes himself as already sinking toward the grave - and at the heart of that description is a single admission: I am a man who has no strength. Strength appears here only as something missing. Whatever vitality he once had is gone, and what is worse, it is gone exactly where he needs it - he has nothing left to push back against the death closing in on him. He feels himself counted among the dead, like the slain lying in a grave, and his emptiness and that living-death are the same condition. The passage does not explain what drained him or offer any relief; it simply reports a man completely emptied out, with no power left inside to resist the end. It is the opposite pole of every other strength in this family - not strength summoned, not strength rising, but strength wholly spent.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is nephesh, here rendered courage - 'their courage melted away in their evil plight': the inmost self read as the seat of nerve, and that nerve dissolving. Type (102) is faculty: courage is treated as a capacity of the inner being, the nephesh functioning as the holder of steadiness - and this reading is unusual in the family for typing the item as a faculty rather than an act or state. Source (103) is absent: the reading does not book an origin for the melting - the storm is in the surrounding verses, but the source-row itself is left empty, so the collapse is reported as an event without a filed cause behind the interior. Seat (104) is none: though nephesh is the inmost self, the reading does not treat the courage as lodged in a distinct interior organ - it is the whole self unnerved, not one faculty-seat failing. Bearer (105) is the sailors (inferred, to_span 269954): the interior of the seafarers who saw the LORD's wondrous works in the deep and were caught in the storm he raised. Operation (106) is 'have courage melt': the event is the dissolving itself - nerve liquefying, the inner steadiness giving way. Target (107) is 'in their plight' (inferred, to_span 269954): the melting happens in the trouble, the evil plight of the heaving sea; the courage fails precisely under the pressure of the danger. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - the collapse is stated plainly, without qualifier. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree of the melting is scored, nothing further particularises it, and no separate outcome is booked - though the next verse has them reeling and staggering at their wits' end, the reading does not file that as this operation's effect. Coupling (112) carries a value (inferred, to_span 269954): it is 'internal:ib-state' - the courage-loss is bound within the inner-being state, welded to the interior condition rather than to an outward companion; the melting is an inside event. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'their courage melted away in their evil plight' - the inmost self unnerved, heart failing as the ship heaved. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the sailors' condition at that moment, the whole crew's nerve giving way. Locus (116) is 'paired with the melting' - the courage is located precisely at the point of its own dissolving; its reference-point is the melting itself, so the reading fixes the item at the instant of collapse. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the sailors' inmost self, tossed up to heaven and down to the depths, loses its nerve - courage melting away under the plight, an inside event bound to the inner state and fixed at the moment of dissolving. This is courage read in descent: not nerve summoned but nerve liquefied, the faculty of steadiness failing when the sea and the fear overwhelm it.
narratives.story: This part of the psalm remembers sailors caught in a storm that God himself stirred up. Their ship is flung up toward the sky and then dropped into the troughs, and the passage turns from the heaving sea to what is happening inside the men: their courage melts away. The inmost self, the place where nerve lives, simply dissolves - their heart fails as the ship pitches. It happens right in the thick of the danger, wrung out of them by the sheer terror of the plight, and it is an inside event, a collapse of the spirit rather than anything on the surface. The passage fixes on the very moment the nerve gives way. Unlike the courage that other psalms summon or that rises in pilgrims on the road, this is courage draining out - steadiness failing exactly when the sea overwhelms it, until the men reel and stagger at their wits' end.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chayil - 'With God we shall do valiantly': valour, doing with strength, the same refrain that closes Psa 60. Type (102) is disposition: here the valour is read as a settled bearing, a standing readiness, rather than as the deed itself - a difference from the Psa 60 reading, which typed it as action. Source (103) is absent: unlike the Psa 60 reading, this one books no separate origin for the valour - the source-row is left empty, so the strength's spring is not filed here even though the verse names God's treading-down of the foes; the reading carries the ground in the target and locus instead. Seat (104) is none: the valour is not organ-located, not lodged in an interior faculty - it is the people's disposition, held by the whole self, not seated in an inner organ. Bearer (105) is 'we (with God)' (inferred, to_span 270102): the collective interior of the people, but named already as the people-with-God, the 'we' who never act apart from him. Operation (106) is 'act valiantly': the event is the valiant doing to which the disposition tends. Target (107) is 'through God' (inferred, to_span 270102): the valour is oriented as something exercised through God - he is the channel and ground of the acting; where the Psa 60 reading booked no target, this one points the valour's exercise explicitly through God. Manner (108) is none: unlike the Psa 60 reading, which marked the manner as 'with God, who treads down the foes', here no mode is separately booked - the 'with God' is carried in the bearer and target rather than filed as manner. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree of the valour is scored, nothing further particularises it, and no separate outcome is booked - the treading-down of foes belongs to God, not filed as this operation's effect. Coupling (112) carries a value (inferred, to_span 270102): it is 'external:god' - the valour is welded to God as its companion and ground; it does not stand alone but is coupled outward to him. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'With God we shall do valiantly' - the courage that is God's gift, valour grounded not in man but in him. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the God-joined people. Locus (116) is 'paired with the vanity of human help' - the valour is located precisely over against the emptiness of man's salvation (v12); its reference-point is the contrast with vain human help, so the reading fixes it as the true alternative to a rescue that fails. The full process: a people who feel rejected by God turn, at the psalm's close, to a valour they hold as a settled disposition - exercised through God, coupled outward to him as its ground, and located as the real answer over against the vanity of human help; courage that is his gift, not their own resource. Read against Psa 60:12, the substance is one - valour grounded in God, not self - but the emphasis has shifted from the deed and God's answering act to the bearing and its God-ward orientation.
narratives.story: This short prayer, almost the same as the close of an earlier psalm, begins in the same discouragement: God seems to have rejected his people and no longer marches with their armies, and human help is worthless. And it ends the same way - with God, they say, we shall do valiantly. Here the courage reads less like a single brave act and more like a settled readiness the people carry, and everything about it points to God: it is exercised through him, bound to him as its ground, held only by a 'we' that is really 'we-with-God'. Most tellingly, it stands exactly opposite the vain human help they had just dismissed - this God-given boldness is the true alternative to a rescue that fails. The courage is real, but it is his gift, not something they generate themselves. Where the earlier psalm stressed the deed and God's crushing of the enemy, this one stresses the steady bearing and the fact that all of it leans on God.
narratives.variation_note: This is the second distinct reading of the refrain 'With God we shall do valiantly' (the first is H2428:valiantly#1 at Psa 60:12), and the difference between them is the finding rather than a repetition to be collapsed. At Psa 60:12 the valour is typed as an ACTION, its SOURCE and MANNER both booked to God ('because it is God who treads down our foes'; 'with God, who treads down the foes'), coupled as the positive counterpart to man's vain salvation, and located as an internal ib-state. Here at Psa 108:13 the same words are typed as a DISPOSITION: source and manner are left unbooked, the valour is oriented 'through God' as target, coupled 'external:god', and located over against 'the vanity of human help'. Both readings ground the valour wholly in God and not in man - the theological substance is identical - but Psa 60 foregrounds the valiant deed and God's answering act, while Psa 108 foregrounds the settled bearing and its God-ward orientation. The near-identical refrain thus yields two facets of one courage: a God-empowered doing and a God-grounded disposition.
